slides.headline: This mammal lays eggs and senses electricity.
slides.sub: The platypus hunts with its eyes shut, and the males carry venom

slides.label: small leathery eggs, the usual platypus clutch
slides.body: The female lays them in a nursery burrow and curls around them. Incubation takes perhaps 6 to 10 days.

slides.headline: It dives with its senses shut down
slides.body: Sight, smell and hearing are essentially shut down while a platypus feeds underwater. It still finds its way perfectly.

slides.headline: The bill reads electricity
slides.body: Electroreceptors and touch receptors in the bill skin pick up the minute electrical signals given off by the muscles of its prey.

slides.headline: Males carry venom
slides.body: A spur on each ankle connects to a venom gland. The venom can kill small animals and cause intense pain in humans.

slides.headline: Milk, but no nipples
slides.body: Females have mammary glands but no nipples. The young suck milk from special mammary hairs for three to four months.

caption:
The platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus) lays eggs, finds prey by electricity and, if male, carries venom in its ankles.

It lives in the rivers and streams of eastern Australia and Tasmania, feeding mostly from dusk to dawn on insect larvae and freshwater crustaceans. Its body runs cool for a mammal, at about 32 °C. After a feed it squeezes back into a burrow so narrow that the entrance presses water out of its fur.

Swipe for all four oddities. Sources on the last slide.

Source: Britannica; Animal Diversity Web; Pettigrew (1999), Journal of Experimental Biology.
